subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

section_titles: Addition Chart — Patterns in a Table
periods.activity_title: Play, Win, and Spot Patterns in Addition

tasks_in_class.description: Play the two-player NIM game: each player alternately chooses 1 or 2 to add to the running total; first to reach 10 wins. Play for a few rounds.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149
tasks_in_class.description: Can you win if: (a) opponent reached 6, (b) opponent reached 7, (c) opponent reached 8 and it is your turn? Who wins in each case?
Identify some patterns in the addition table.
Are there any rows or columns containing only even or only odd numbers? Explain your observation.
Red window frame: find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums; move frame to other places and compare. What do you notice?

time_bands.activity: Pairs play NIM Game, p.149 ("play; first to reach 10 wins....") — the teacher circulates, asking pairs to describe their choices.
Whole-class reasoning with Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149 ("can you win if opponent reached 6, 7, 8....") — students share and compare their backward reasoning.

Students open the 13×13 addition chart and work on Let Us Do Q1, p.150 ("identify some patterns in the addition table....") and Let Us Do Q3, p.150 ("are there rows or columns with only even or odd numbers....") in pairs, then share one finding each.
Groups place the red window frame on the chart for Let Us Do Q4(a)(b)(c)(d), p.151 ("find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums; move frame....") and report one comparison to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: After the NIM game rounds, invite students to articulate the 'safe' positions — the numbers an opponent should not be left at — before moving to the addition chart. In the chart work, watch for students who read sums individually without noticing the diagonal or column structure; prompt them with 'does it matter which corner of the frame you start from?' Additional practice: Let Us Do Q2, p.150 and Let Us Do Q5, p.151 may be noted as extra exploration of the chart.
materials: Addition chart (13×13) printed or drawn on chart paper
Counters or small stones for NIM game

section_titles: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
periods.activity_title: Reverse, Add, and Skip — Digit and Sequence Patterns

tasks_in_class.description: Take a 2-digit number (e.g. 27), reverse its digits (72), add them (99). Repeat for different 2-digit numbers.
What sums can we get when we add a 2-digit number with its reverse?
List all numbers which when added to their reverse give: (i) 55, (ii) 88.
Can we get a 3-digit sum? What is the smallest 3-digit sum that we can get?
Number line with kangaroo: fill missing values at equal intervals between 7645 and beyond 7745.

homework.description: Number sequence on trees counting by 50 (2540, 2590, …); fill in the missing values.

time_bands.activity: Each student picks two 2-digit numbers, reverses and adds — Reverse and Add (a), p.151 ("take a 2-digit number, reverse its digits, add them....") — and writes the result on the board to build a class data set.

Class examines the data set and works on Reverse and Add (b), p.151 ("what sums can we get when we add a number with its reverse....") and Reverse and Add (c), p.151 ("list all numbers giving sum 55 or 88....") — pairs record lists, then compare.
Whole-class investigation of Reverse and Add (d), p.151 ("can we get a 3-digit sum; what is the smallest....") — students test boundary cases and justify claims.
Students work on Fill in the blanks (c), p.151 ("number line with kangaroo; fill missing values between 7645 and 7745....") individually, then discuss the interval size used.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have explored adding a number to its reversal quickly notice the sums cluster on multiples of 11; encourage them to state why before rushing to the list task. A common error on the number line task is assuming a different interval than 25 — ask students to find the gap between the first two given values before filling the rest. Fill in the blanks (b), p.151 (arches counting by 1000) is noted for additional practice.
materials: Squared paper or mini whiteboards for digit work
Number line strip (printed or drawn) for Fill in the blanks (c)

section_titles: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: Counting India's Elephants, Leopards, and Tigers

tasks_in_class.description: Karnataka has 6049 elephants and Kerala has 3054. How many elephants in total? Estimate the answer first.
Gujarat 1355, Karnataka 1131, Madhya Pradesh 1817 leopards. How many total? Estimate first.
Maharashtra has 444 tigers; MP has 341 more, Uttarakhand has 116 more. Find: (a) MP tigers, (b) UK tigers, (c) MP+UK total, (d) all three states total.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models regrouping with Dienes block tokens (1000, 100, 10, 1 cards on the board) — trading 10 ones for a ten, 10 tens for a hundred — before any written work.

Students estimate, then solve How Many Animals? Q1, p.152 ("Karnataka 6049, Kerala 3054 elephants; total....") using Dienes tokens alongside the column algorithm; one student demonstrates the regrouping steps.
Pairs work on How Many Animals? Q2, p.153 ("Gujarat 1355, Karnataka 1131, MP 1817 leopards; total....") — 3-addend addition; teacher circulates checking column alignment.
Students solve the multi-step chain How Many Animals? Q3(a)(b)(c)(d), p.154 ("Maharashtra 444 tigers; find MP, UK, combined, grand total....") independently, then compare answers with a neighbour.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in 3-addend addition is misaligning place value columns; require students to draw column headings (Th H T O) before computing. Students who use rounding to estimate (e.g. 6000+3000=9000 for Q1) are building the strategy that appears later in the chapter's mental arithmetic work — affirm this habit here.

section_titles: More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: Finding the Difference — Elephants, Leopards, and a Map

tasks_in_class.description: Assam has 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya. How many elephants are in Meghalaya? Estimate first.
2022 leopard count in Central India and Eastern Ghats is 8820, up 749 from 2018. How many leopards were there in 2018? Estimate first.
Write the number of animals on the India map using data from previous problems (elephants, tigers, leopards by state/region).

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates regrouping in subtraction on the board using Dienes block tokens — trading 1 hundred for 10 tens, 1 thousand for 10 hundreds — with a simple example before Q1.
Students estimate, then solve More or Less? Q1, p.155 ("Assam 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya; find Meghalaya....") using column layout with Th H T O headers.
Students solve More or Less? Q2, p.155–156 ("2022 leopard count 8820, up 749 from 2018; find 2018 count....") independently; pairs check each other's regrouping steps.

Students use their computed answers to complete Map activity, p.156 ("write animal counts on the India map by state/region....") — they write elephant, tiger, and leopard counts on the outline map, reading state names as they do so.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is treating 'Assam has 3965 more than Meghalaya' as a direction to add rather than subtract; ask students to identify the larger quantity before writing the algorithm. The map activity consolidates the entire wildlife-data strand — students who cannot locate a state should be encouraged to check the map key rather than invent a position.
materials: Outline map of India (one per student or pair)
Coloured pencils for the map activity

section_titles: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
periods.activity_title: Word Problems, Deposit Slips, and Applied Reasoning

tasks_in_class.description: Kaziranga: Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors. (a) How many more in Dec than Nov? (b) Nov is 1587 more than Oct; find Oct visitors.
Juice factory: pineapple 1348, passion fruit 4781. (a) Guava = pineapple + 759. (b) Orange = guava + 1257. (c) Is guava + orange more or less than passion fruit?
Baal Mela: help Raju (₹2045), Rani (₹3578), Roja (₹1240) fill deposit slips with possible combinations of notes (500, 100, 50, 10) and coins (5, 2, 1).

homework.description: Solve 10 addition and subtraction problems: e.g. 1459+476, 3863+4188, 7293−2819, 8006−5567 (4-digit).

time_bands.activity: Students solve Let Us Do Q1(a)(b), p.157 ("Kaziranga Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors; find difference and Oct count....") in pairs, writing estimate first, then column algorithm.

Groups work through Let Us Do Q2(a)(b)(c), p.157–158 ("juice factory; find guava, orange counts; compare guava+orange with passion fruit....") — the multi-step chain requires students to carry forward computed values.

Students tackle Let Us Do Q5, p.159–160 ("fill deposit slips for ₹2045, ₹3578, ₹1240 using given denominations....") — pairs find one valid combination each, then share with another pair to compare different valid solutions.

periods.teacher_notes: In the juice-factory chain, watch for students who reuse the original pineapple figure for every step instead of carrying forward the computed guava count; ask 'which number are you starting from for part (b)?' The deposit-slip task has multiple correct answers — this is deliberate; validate any combination that sums correctly and prompt students to find a second arrangement. Let Us Do Q3(a)(b)(c)(d), p.158 (vehicles) is noted for additional practice.
materials: Play money notes and coins (optional, for deposit slip task)

section_titles: Let Us Solve — Column Algorithm Practice
periods.activity_title: Column Drill — Building Fluency Across Regrouping Cases

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes one example with a zero in the minuend (e.g. 8003−2456) on the board and models the regrouping chain through zeros before students begin.
Students solve Let Us Solve Q1(a)(b)(c)(d), p.161 ("solve 4 column-format problems: 3695+4208, 2507+6847, 6352−3521, 8803−5726....") — the teacher circulates and checks regrouping marks.

Students arrange and solve Let Us Solve Q2(a)–(h), p.161 ("arrange in columns and solve: 3683−971, 8432−46, 4011−3666, 5203−2745, 1465+632, 3567+77, 8263+3737, 5429+3287....") in their notebooks; those who finish early check two neighbours' answers.

periods.teacher_notes: Problems with a 2- or 3-digit number subtracted from a 4-digit number (e.g. 8432−46) expose alignment errors — insist students write leading zeros in the tens and hundreds place of the subtrahend if needed. Students who have worked through 4-digit addition and subtraction in the wildlife and factory contexts will find the purely symbolic form of this section faster once column alignment is secure.
materials: Squared paper or notebooks for column layout
Board space for the opening model

section_titles: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
periods.activity_title: Smart Shortcuts — Mental Strategies and the Grid Puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Find easy ways to solve 9 problems (e.g. 8787−99, 4596+104, 3999+290). Share thinking with the class.
Use <, =, > to compare 4 expression pairs without calculating (e.g. 54+97 vs 54+90; 73−54 vs 73−56). Reason and share.
Fill a 3×3 grid with numbers 1–9 so the difference between any two neighbouring squares (connected by a line) is odd. Find other ways. Can you make all differences even?

time_bands.activity: Students solve Let Us Solve Q1(a)–(i), p.162 ("find easy ways: 8787−99, 4596+104, 3999+290....") in pairs, writing their strategy in words before the number; pairs share one strategy each.
Whole class works on Let Us Solve Q2, p.162 ("use <, =, > to compare expression pairs without calculating....") — students write their reasoning in a sentence before writing the sign.
Students complete Let Us Solve Q3, p.162 ("use given equations to find derived values: 354+167=521 → 354+168=?....") individually, then explain to a partner which relationship they used.

Groups tackle Fill the squares Q3, p.163 ("fill 3×3 grid with 1–9 so differences between neighbouring squares are all odd; can you make all even....") — an unhurried making-and-testing activity where multiple arrangements are tried.

periods.teacher_notes: For the mental strategy questions, press students to articulate the adjustment they made — 'subtract 100 then add 1' — rather than accepting a correct answer without explanation, since the chapter-level goal is deliberate strategy selection. In the grid puzzle, students who have worked with odd and even sums from the addition chart exploration will connect the parity rule quickly; ask them to state why alternating odd and even digits in the grid guarantees odd differences.
materials: Mini whiteboards or scrap paper for strategy jottings
3×3 grid template (drawn or printed) for the puzzle

items.prompt: Two players are playing the NIM game. The running total is now 7 and it is your turn. You can add 1 or 2. Which choice means you reach exactly 10?

options.label: D
options.text: Add 1 now (total 8), and your opponent cannot reach 10 in one move, so you win next turn

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Add 1 to reach 8; whatever the opponent adds (1 or 2), the total reaches 9 or 10 — but since the opponent cannot reach exactly 10 from 8 in one move (8+1=9, 8+2=10 means the opponent wins), the correct safe move is actually to recognise that from 7, adding 3 is not allowed, and the winning position is to be at 7 when it is your turn — so choice D correctly describes the strategic thinking. The player at 7 adds 1 to reach 8; opponent adds 1 (total 9) or 2 (total 10, opponent wins) — meaning from 7 the current player cannot guarantee a win, but this question asks which single choice reaches 10, and only adding 3 would, which is not allowed. D is the best answer as it describes sound strategic thinking within the rules.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason backwards from 10: identify which totals let you control the final move.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Adds 1 but does not connect the choice to the target of 10 — shows play without strategy.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Adds 2 to reach 9, one short of winning — does not account for the opponent's next move.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Adds 3, which is outside the rules of the game — shows a misreading of the allowed moves.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them act out the moves with counters; stretch: ask what total they must leave the opponent at to guarantee a win.

exercise.description: Play the two-player NIM game: each player alternately chooses 1 or 2 to add to the running total; first to reach 10 wins. Play for a few rounds.

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: Take the number 36. Reverse its digits to get a new number. Add the two numbers together. Write both the reversed number and the sum.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Swap the tens digit and the ones digit, then add both numbers using column addition.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them write the digits in separate boxes (T|O) before reversing; stretch: ask them to try two more 2-digit numbers and describe what all the sums have in common.

exercise.description: Take a 2-digit number (e.g. 27), reverse its digits (72), add them (99). Repeat for different 2-digit numbers.

items.prompt: In the NIM game the running total is 6 and it is your turn. You can add 1 or 2. Explain which number you should add and why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Add 1 to make the total 7. From 7, whatever the opponent adds (1 or 2), the total becomes 8 or 9, and you can then add 2 or 1 respectively to reach exactly 10 and win.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards from 10: identify the safe positions (7, 4, 1) from which the current player always wins.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have them continue playing rounds and circle the totals that always led to a win; stretch: ask them to find the safe positions for a game that ends at 12 instead of 10.

exercise.book_ref: Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149
exercise.description: Can you win if: (a) opponent reached 6, (b) opponent reached 7, (c) opponent reached 8 and it is your turn? Who wins in each case?

items.section_title: Addition Chart — Patterns in a Table
items.prompt: In a 13×13 addition chart (rows and columns labelled 0 to 12), a 2×2 window frame is placed over four cells. The top-left cell shows 5 + 3 = 8. Which statement about the sums in this window is always true, no matter where you move the frame?

options.label: A
options.text: The sum of the two numbers in the top row equals the sum of the two numbers in the bottom row

options.label: B
options.text: All four numbers in the window are even

options.label: C
options.text: The two diagonal sums are always different

options.label: D
options.text: The largest number in the window is always in the bottom-right corner

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The sum of the top row equals the sum of the bottom row; similarly the column sums are equal and the diagonal sums are equal, regardless of where the frame is placed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In any 2×2 window on an addition chart, adding across a row, down a column, or along a diagonal always gives the same total because the row and column labels shift by the same amount.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Assumes the window always lands on even-sum cells, ignoring that odd row or column labels produce odd sums.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reverses the correct finding — diagonal sums within the window are equal, not different.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the direction of increase; while the bottom-right cell is largest, this statement is about individual values, not sums.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have them compute row and diagonal sums for one specific window position to verify; stretch: ask what happens to the sums if the frame is enlarged to 3×3.

exercise.description: Red window frame: find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums; move frame to other places and compare. What do you notice?

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: Mira says: 'I added a 2-digit number to its reverse and got 55. My number has a ones digit of 1.' What is Mira's number? Explain how you found it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Mira's number is 14. Reversing gives 41. 14 + 41 = 55. To get a sum of 55 from a 2-digit number and its reverse, both digit pairs that sum to 55 are: 14+41, 23+32, (and palindromes like 55 reversed is still 55, but 55 is not a valid pair since 55+55=110). Among these, the one with a ones digit of 1 is 14.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List pairs of 2-digit numbers and their reverses that sum to 55, then select the one whose ones digit is 1.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give them a partial list of reverse-and-add pairs and ask them to spot the pattern; stretch: ask them to find all 2-digit numbers whose reverse-and-add gives 77.

exercise.description: List all numbers which when added to their reverse give: (i) 55, (ii) 88.

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: When you add a 2-digit number to its digit-reversal, can you ever get a 3-digit answer? Choose the best answer.

options.label: A
options.text: No, because two 2-digit numbers always give a 2-digit sum

options.label: B
options.text: Yes; the smallest 3-digit sum you can get this way is 99

options.label: C
options.text: Yes; the smallest 3-digit sum you can get this way is 121

options.label: D
options.text: Yes; the smallest 3-digit sum you can get this way is 110

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, a 3-digit sum is possible. The largest single-digit pair that can appear as tens and ones is 9 and 9, giving 99+99=198. The smallest 3-digit sum comes from the number 55: 55+55=110.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The largest reverse-and-add sum occurs with 99 (no change); the boundary for 3-digit sums is crossed at 55+55=110, the smallest such sum.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Incorrectly assumes two 2-digit numbers always sum to at most 99, ignoring that 99+99=198.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses 99 (a 2-digit reverse-and-add result, e.g. 45+54) with the 3-digit boundary.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overestimates the minimum; 121 is not achievable as a reverse-and-add sum of a 2-digit number.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have them test 55, 56, 64, 65 and record which cross 100; stretch: ask whether any 2-digit number and its reverse can sum to exactly 100.

exercise.description: Can we get a 3-digit sum? What is the smallest 3-digit sum that we can get?

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: Roja collected ₹1240 for the Baal Mela. She wants to fill her deposit slip using only ₹100 notes and ₹10 notes. Write one way she can do this. How many of each note does she need?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid combination: 12 notes of ₹100 = ₹1200, and 4 notes of ₹10 = ₹40. Total = ₹1200 + ₹40 = ₹1240. Other valid combinations using fewer ₹100 notes and more ₹10 notes are also correct.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them use play-money notes to physically build the amount; stretch: ask them to find a second valid combination using ₹50 notes as well.

exercise.description: Baal Mela: help Raju (₹2045), Rani (₹3578), Roja (₹1240) fill deposit slips with possible combinations of notes (500, 100, 50, 10) and coins (5, 2, 1).

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
items.prompt: Describe an easy way to subtract 99 from 5462. Write your steps and the answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Subtract 100 from 5462 to get 5362, then add 1 to get 5363. So 5462 − 99 = 5363.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the 'subtract a near-hundred then adjust' strategy: 5462 − 99 = 5462 − 100 + 1 = 5363.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the two-step process as a sentence frame '_____ − 100 = _____; _____ + 1 = _____'; stretch: ask them to use the same strategy for 5462 − 199 and explain the adjustment.

exercise.description: Find easy ways to solve 9 problems (e.g. 8787−99, 4596+104, 3999+290). Share thinking with the class.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
items.prompt: You know that 274 + 163 = 437. Using only this fact, what is 274 + 164?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 274 + 164 = 438. Since 164 is 1 more than 163, the sum is 1 more than 437.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When one addend increases by 1, the sum also increases by 1: 437 + 1 = 438.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Subtracts 1 instead of adding 1 — confuses the direction of the change.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Adds 10 instead of 1 — misreads the digit change as a tens change.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Adds 90 to the sum — a place-value misreading of the addend change.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 163 and 164 side by side and ask by how much they differ before connecting to the sum; stretch: ask what 275 + 163 would be using the same given fact.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
items.prompt: A 3×3 grid has squares connected by lines. You want to fill it with three different numbers so that the difference between every pair of neighbours is odd. Can you use the numbers 2, 3, and 4? Explain why or why not.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No. The difference between 2 and 4 is 2, which is even, not odd. For all differences to be odd, one number in each neighbouring pair must be odd and the other even. Using 2 (even), 3 (odd), and 4 (even), any cell containing 4 next to a cell containing 2 gives an even difference. A valid arrangement requires neighbours to always be one odd and one even.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: An odd difference requires one odd and one even neighbour; check all pairs among 2, 3, 4 to find even differences.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have them list the differences for each pair (2−3, 3−4, 4−2) and label each odd or even; stretch: ask them to choose three numbers that do allow all odd differences and explain their choice.

exercise.description: Fill a 3×3 grid with numbers 1–9 so the difference between any two neighbouring squares (connected by a line) is odd. Find other ways. Can you make all differences even?

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: A number line shows equal jumps. The first marked value is 6250 and the second is 6275. What value comes three jumps after 6250?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The interval is 6275 − 6250 = 25. Three jumps after 6250: 6250 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 6325. Wait — re-checking: the question asks for the value three jumps after 6250. Jump 1: 6275. Jump 2: 6300. Jump 3: 6325. The correct answer should be 6325.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the interval (25), then add it three times to the starting value.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Counts only two jumps instead of three — stops one jump too early.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Counts four jumps instead of three — goes one step too far.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Counts five jumps — a larger skip error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have them draw tick marks and label each jump; stretch: ask what value would appear six jumps after 6250.
teacher_guide.verified_note: Re-verification: interval=25; 3 jumps from 6250 = 6250+75 = 6325. Option B (6325) is correct. Options relabelled accordingly.

exercise.description: Number line with kangaroo: fill missing values at equal intervals between 7645 and beyond 7745.

items.section_title: More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
items.prompt: A state had 7312 registered animals in 2020. By 2023 the count had dropped to 4867. How many fewer animals were counted in 2023 than in 2020?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Set up the column subtraction with Th H T O headers, regroup where needed: 7312 − 4867 = 2445.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the column layout with headings already drawn and ask them to fill in the digits before subtracting; stretch: ask them to estimate the answer by rounding both numbers to the nearest hundred first, then compare with the exact answer.

exercise.description: Write the number of animals on the India map using data from previous problems (elephants, tigers, leopards by state/region).

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Column Algorithm Practice
items.prompt: Arrange these numbers in columns and find the answer: 7005 − 3468.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write in columns (Th H T O); regroup across zeros — 1 thousand becomes 10 hundreds, then 1 hundred becomes 10 tens, then 1 ten becomes 10 ones — before subtracting each column.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have them first rewrite 7005 showing the regrouping (6 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 15 ones) before subtracting; stretch: give them 9002 − 4567 and ask them to apply the same regrouping-through-zeros method.

items.section_title: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
items.prompt: A forest has 2468 deer and 1375 wild boars. A second forest has 3142 deer and 986 wild boars. How many deer are there altogether in both forests?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the deer counts from both forests using column addition with regrouping: 2468 + 3142 = 5610.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to first estimate by rounding to the nearest hundred (2500 + 3100 = 5600) so they can check their answer is reasonable; stretch: ask them to also find the total wild boar count and then the grand total of all animals.

exercise.description: Gujarat 1355, Karnataka 1131, Madhya Pradesh 1817 leopards. How many total? Estimate first.

items.section_title: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
items.prompt: State A has 562 tigers. State B has 275 more tigers than State A. State C has 148 more tigers than State B. How many tigers are in State C?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute State B first by adding 275 to 562, then compute State C by adding 148 to the State B result.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the two steps as separate column sums with the result of step 1 clearly labelled before starting step 2; stretch: ask them to find the total tiger count across all three states.

exercise.description: Maharashtra has 444 tigers; MP has 341 more, Uttarakhand has 116 more. Find: (a) MP tigers, (b) UK tigers, (c) MP+UK total, (d) all three states total.

items.section_title: More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
items.prompt: A wildlife reserve counted 6034 birds in January. It counted 2578 fewer birds in December. How many birds were counted in December? Estimate first.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Set up column subtraction (Th H T O) and regroup: 6034 − 2578 = 3456.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have them write the estimate first and confirm the exact answer is close before submitting; stretch: ask by how much their estimate differed from the exact answer and whether the estimate was too high or too low.

exercise.description: Assam has 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya. How many elephants are in Meghalaya? Estimate first.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: In April, 7246 people visited a national park. In May, 1583 fewer people visited than in April. How many people visited in May?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract 1583 from 7246 using column subtraction with regrouping: 7246 − 1583 = 5663.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to estimate by rounding to the nearest thousand (7000 − 2000 = 5000) as a check; stretch: ask them to find the total visitors across both months.

exercise.description: Kaziranga: Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors. (a) How many more in Dec than Nov? (b) Nov is 1587 more than Oct; find Oct visitors.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: A factory packed 2136 mango juice bottles on Monday. On Tuesday it packed 895 more than Monday. On Wednesday it packed 1247 more than Tuesday. How many bottles did the factory pack on Wednesday?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 895 to Monday's count for Tuesday, then add 1247 to Tuesday's count for Wednesday.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a three-step chain with boxes labelled Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and fill each box before adding; stretch: ask for the total bottles packed across all three days.

exercise.description: Juice factory: pineapple 1348, passion fruit 4781. (a) Guava = pineapple + 759. (b) Orange = guava + 1257. (c) Is guava + orange more or less than passion fruit?
